# AF 第六章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 6

[P01] All that year the animals worked like slaves. But they were happy in their work; they did not grudge any effort or sacrifice, well aware that everything they did was for themselves and for those of their kind who would come after them, and not for a pack of idle, thieving human beings. Throughout the spring and summer they worked a sixty hour week, and in August Napoleon announced that there would be work on Sunday afternoons as well. All through the spring and summer they worked a sixty-hour week, and in August Napoleon announced that there would be work on Sunday afternoons too. This work was strictly voluntary, but any animal who stayed away would have his rations（配给） cut by half.

[P02] Even so, some tasks had to be left undone（毁掉）. The harvest was a little less successful than the year before, and two fields that should have been sown（播种） with roots in the early summer were not sown, because the ploughing had not been finished early enough. One could foresee（预见） that the coming winter would be hard. This work was strictly voluntary, but any animal who stayed away would have his rations cut by half. The windmill（风车） brought unexpected（意外） difficulties. There was a good quarry（采石场） of limestone（石灰石） on the farm, and plenty of sand and cement（水泥） had been found in one of the outhouses（外屋）, so all the materials for building were close at hand.

[P03] But the first problem the animals could not solve was how to break the stone into right-sized pieces. There seemed no way except with picks and crowbars（铁撬）, which no animal could use, because none could stand on his hind（后面的） legs. Only after weeks of useless（无用） effort did the right idea come—to use the force of gravity（重力）. Huge boulders（巨石）, too big to be used as they were, lay all over the quarry floor. The animals tied ropes round them, and all together—cows, horses, sheep, any animal that could hold the rope—dragged（拖） them with desperate（绝望） slowness（缓慢） up the slope（斜坡） to the top, where they were pushed over the edge to break below.

[P04] Moving the stone once it was broken was comparatively（比较地） simple. The horses carried it off in cart-loads（负载）, the sheep dragged single blocks, even Muriel and Benjamin put themselves into an old governess（女教师）-cart and did their share. By late summer a sufficient（足够） store of stone had piled up, and then the building began, under the direction of the pigs. But it was a slow, laborious（辛苦） process. Frequently, it took a whole day of exhausting effort to drag a single boulder（巨石） to the top of the quarry, and sometimes when it was pushed over the edge it failed to break.

[P05] Nothing could be done without Boxer, whose strength seemed equal to all the other animals put together. When the boulder began to slip（滑） and the animals cried out in despair（绝望） as they were dragged down the hill, it was always Boxer who pulled hard against the rope and stopped the boulder. To see him toiling（苦干） up the slope inch by inch, breathing fast, the tips of his hoofs（蹄） clawing（抓） at the ground, and his great sides wet with sweat（汗水）, filled everyone with admiration（钦佩）. Clover warned him sometimes to be careful not to overstrain（过度劳损） himself, but Boxer would never listen to her.

[P06] His two slogans, "I will work harder" and "Napoleon is always right," seemed to him a sufficient answer to all problems. He had arranged（安排） with the cockerel（小公鸡） to call him three-quarters（住处） of an hour earlier in the mornings. And in his spare moments, he would go alone to the quarry, collect a load（负载） of broken stone, and drag it down to the windmill without help. The animals were not badly off that summer, in spite（恶意） of the hardness（硬度） of their work. If they had no more food than in Jones's day, at least they did not have less.

[P07] The advantage of only having to feed themselves, and not having to support five wasteful（浪费） humans as well, was so great that many failures（失败） would not outweigh（超过） it. And in many ways the animals' way of doing things was better and saved work. Jobs like weeding（除草）, for example, could be done more thoroughly（彻底） than humans ever could. And also, since no animal stole now, there was no need to fence off pasture（牧场） from crop land, which saved much work on hedges（树篱） and gates. Still, as the summer went on, different unexpected shortages began to be felt.

[P08] They needed paraffin（石蜡） oil, nails（钉子）, string, dog biscuits, and iron for the horses' shoes, none of which could be made on the farm. Later they would also need seeds and artificial manure（肥料）, besides different tools and, finally, the machinery（机器） for the windmill. How these were to be got, no one was able to imagine. The good of only having to feed themselves, and not having to support five wasteful humans as well, was so great that many failures would not outweigh it. One Sunday morning, when the animals gathered（聚集） to receive their orders, Napoleon announced that he had decided on a new policy（政策）.

[P09] From now on Animal Farm would trade with the neighbouring farms: not, of course, for any commercial（商业） purpose, but simply to obtain（获得） certain materials which were urgently（紧急） necessary. The needs of the windmill must override（压倒） everything else, he said. He was therefore making arrangements（安排） to sell a stack（堆） of hay（干草） and part of this year's wheat crop, and later, if more money were needed, it would have to be made up by selling eggs, for which there was always a market in Willingdon. The hens, said Napoleon, should welcome this sacrifice as their own special contribution towards the building of the windmill. Once again the animals were conscious（意识到） of a vague（模糊） uneasiness（不安）.

[P10] Never to have any dealings（交易） with human beings, never to engage（从事） in trade, never to use money—had not these been among the earliest（最早） resolutions passed at that first triumphant（得意） Meeting after Jones was expelled（驱逐）? All the animals remembered passing such resolutions, or at least they thought so. The four young pigs who had protested（抗议） when Napoleon abolished（废除） the Meetings raised their voices timidly（胆怯）, but the dogs silenced them at once with a tremendous（极大的） growling（咆哮）. Then, as usual, the sheep broke into "Four legs good, two legs bad!" and the awkwardness（尴尬） was smoothed over. Finally Napoleon raised his trotter（猪蹄） for silence and announced that he had already made all the arrangements.

[P11] There would be no need for any of the animals to come into contact with human beings, which would clearly be most undesirable（不受欢迎）. He meant to take the whole burden（负担） on his own shoulders. Whymper, a solicitor（律师） living in Willingdon, had agreed to act as go-between between Animal Farm and the outside world, and would visit the farm every Monday morning to receive his orders. Napoleon ended his speech with his usual cry of "Long live Animal Farm!" and after the singing of 'animals of England' the animals were dismissed（驳回）.

[P12] He assured（保证） them that the resolution against engaging（迷人） in trade and using money had never been passed, or even suggested. It was pure imagination, probably coming at first from lies spread by Snowball. A few animals still felt a little doubtful（怀疑的）, but Squealer asked them cleverly, "Are you certain that this is not something that you have dreamed, comrades（同志们）? Have you any record of such a resolution? Is it written down anywhere?" Every Monday Mr. Whymper visited the farm, and since it was certainly true that nothing of the kind existed in writing, the animals were satisfied that they had been mistaken. Every Monday Mr. Whymper visited the farm as had been arranged.

[P13] He was a sly（狡猾的）-looking little man with side whiskers（胡须）, a solicitor with very little business, but sharp（锋利） enough to see before anyone else that Animal Farm would need a broker and that the commissions（佣金） would be worth having. The animals watched him come and go with dread（恐惧）, and stayed away as much as possible. Nevertheless, the sight of Napoleon on all fours giving orders to Whymper, who stood on two legs, woke their pride and made them partly accept the new arrangement. Their relations with the human race were now not quite the same. The human beings did not hate Animal Farm less now that it was prosperous（繁荣的）; indeed, they hated it more than ever.

[P14] Every human held it as a fact of faith（信任） that the farm would go bankrupt（破产） sooner or later, and, above all, that the windmill would be a failure（失败）. They would meet in the public-houses and prove by diagrams（图表） that the windmill was sure to fall down, or that if it did stand up, then that it would never work. Yet, against their will, they had developed a certain respect for the efficiency（效率） with which the animals were managing their own affairs（事务）. One sign was that they had begun to call Animal Farm by its proper name and stopped pretending that it was called the farm Farm.

[P15] They had also stopped supporting Jones, who had given up hope of getting his farm back and gone to live in another part of the county（县）. Except through Whymper, there was still no contact between Animal Farm and the outside world, but there were constant（不断） rumours（谣言） that Napoleon was about to make a definite（确定） business agreement either with Mr. Pilkington of Foxwood（狐林） or with Mr. Frederick of Pinchfield（窄地）--but never, it was noticed, with both at the same time. It was about this time that the pigs suddenly moved into the farmhouse（农舍） and took up their residence（住所） there.

[P16] Again the animals seemed to remember that a resolution against this had been passed early on, and again Squealer convinced（确信） them that this was not the case. It was necessary, he said, that the pigs, the cleverest on the farm, should have a quiet place to work in. It was also more suited to the dignity（尊严） of the Leader (for lately he had taken to speaking of Napoleon as "Leader") to live in a house than in a mere（仅仅） pigsty（猪圈）. Nevertheless（然而）, some animals were worried when they heard that the pigs not only ate in the kitchen and used the sitting-room as a game room, but also slept in the beds.

[P17] Boxer passed it off as usual with "Napoleon is always right!", but Clover, who thought she remembered a clear ruling against beds, went to the end of the barn（谷仓） and tried to puzzle（谜） out the Seven Commandments（戒律） written there. Finding she could read only single letters, she fetched Muriel. "Muriel," she said, "read me the Fourth Commandment（戒律）. Does it not say something about never sleeping in a bed?" With some difficulty Muriel spelt（拼写） it out. "It says, 'No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets（床单）,'" she announced finally. Strangely enough, Clover had not remembered that the Fourth Commandment mentioned sheets; but as it was there on the wall, it must have done so.

[P18] And Squealer, who happened to pass by just then, with two or three dogs beside him, was able to explain the whole matter clearly. "You have heard then, comrades," he said, "that we pigs now sleep in the beds of the farmhouse? And why not? You did not suppose, surely, that there was ever a rule against beds? A bed just means a place to sleep in. A pile of straw（稻草） in a stall（畜栏） is a bed, if you look at it right. The rule was against sheets, which are a human invention. We have taken the sheets off the farmhouse beds, and sleep between blankets（毯子）.

[P19] And they are very comfortable beds too! But not more comfortable than we need, comrades, with all the brainwork（脑力劳动） we have to do nowadays. You would not rob（抢劫） us of our rest, would you? You would not have us too tired to do our duties? Surely none of you wishes to see Jones back?" The animals reassured him at once that surely none of them wished to see Jones back, and no more was said about the pigs sleeping in the farmhouse beds. And when, some days later, it was announced that the pigs would get up an hour later than the other animals, no complaint（抱怨） was made either. By the autumn the animals were tired but happy.

[P20] They had had a hard year, and after they sold part of the hay and corn, the food stores for winter were not too plentiful（丰富）, but the windmill made up for everything. It was almost half built now. After the harvest came a long stretch（伸展） of clear dry weather, and the animals toiled（苦干） harder than ever, thinking it worth while to plod（跋涉） to and fro（来回） all day with blocks of stone if they could raise the walls another foot. Boxer would even come out at nights and work alone by the light of the harvest moon. In their spare moments the animals would walk round the half-finished mill（磨坊）, admiring the strength and uprightness（正直） of its walls and wondering that they could ever have built anything so imposing（壮观）.

[P21] Only old Benjamin refused to get excited about the windmill, though, as usual, he would say nothing except the cryptic（神秘） remark（评论） that donkeys live a long time. November came, with wild south-west winds. Building had to stop because it was now too wet to mix the cement. At last there came a night when the gale（大风） was so strong that the farm buildings shook on their foundations（地基） and several tiles（瓦片） were blown off the roof of the barn. The hens woke up squawking（尖叫） with terror（恐怖） because they had all dreamed at the same time of hearing a gun go off in the distance.

[P22] In the morning the animals came out of their stalls（畜栏） and found that the flagstaff（旗杆） had been blown down and an elm（榆树） tree at the foot of the orchard（果园） had been plucked（采摘） up like a radish（萝卜）. They had just noticed this when a cry of despair broke from every animal's throat. A terrible sight met their eyes. The windmill was in ruins（废墟）. With one accord（一致） they dashed（猛冲） down to the spot（地点）. Napoleon, who seldom moved faster than a walk, raced ahead of them all. Yes, there it lay, the fruit of all their struggles（斗争）, levelled to its foundations, the stones they had broken and carried so laboriously（费力） scattered（散落） all around.

[P23] Unable（无法） at first to speak, they stood gazing（凝视） mournfully（悲伤） at the fallen stone. Napoleon paced（踱步） in silence, sometimes snuffing（嗅） at the ground. His tail had grown rigid（僵硬） and twitched（抽搐） sharply（尖锐地）, a sign of strong thought. Suddenly he stopped as though his mind were made up. "Comrades," he said quietly, "do you know who is responsible? Do you know the enemy who came in the night and threw down our windmill? SNOWBALL!" he roared（吼叫） in a voice of thunder. "Snowball has done this! In sheer malice（恶意）, to set back our plans and avenge（复仇） his shameful（可耻） expulsion（驱逐）, this traitor crept（爬行） here under cover of night and destroyed our work of nearly a year.

[P24] Comrades, here and now I give the death sentence on Snowball. 'Animal Hero, Second Class,' and half a bushel（蒲式耳） of apples to any animal who brings him to justice. A full bushel to anyone who captures him alive!" The animals were shocked beyond measure（测量） to learn that even Snowball could do such a thing. They cried out in anger, and everyone began to think of ways to catch Snowball if he ever came back. Almost at once the footprints（脚印） of a pig were found in the grass a little way from the knoll（小丘）. They could only be followed for a few yards, but seemed to lead to a hole in the hedge（树篱）.

[P25] Napoleon snuffed（嗅） deeply at them and said they were Snowball's. He said Snowball had probably come from the direction of Foxwood Farm. "No more delays（延迟）, comrades!" cried Napoleon when the footprints had been examined. "There is work to be done. This very morning we begin rebuilding the windmill, and we will build all through the winter, rain or shine. We will teach this miserable（悲惨的） traitor that he cannot undo（取消） our work so easily. Remember, comrades, there must be no change in our plans: they shall be carried out to the day. Forward, comrades! Long live the windmill!

[P26] Long live Animal Farm!
